### Summary

A security vulnerability has been identified in GitHub CLI that could allow attestation verification bypass when using `gh attestation verify` with `--signer-repo` or `--signer-workflow` flags. GitHub CLI builds the certificate matcher from these flag values without escaping regex metacharacters, so a repository or workflow name is treated as a regular expression rather than a literal string. GitHub permits characters such as  `.`  in organization, repository, and workflow path names, and  `.`  is a regex wildcard, so a malicious actor can create a lookalike name that satisfies a matcher intended for a different, trusted signer.

### Details

GitHub CLI constructs a regular expression from the  `--signer-repo`  and  `--signer-workflow`  values and matches it against the signing certificate's SAN (Subject Alternative Name) during Sigstore attestation verification. The user-supplied value is interpolated into the pattern without escaping regex metacharacters, so any metacharacter permitted in a GitHub path is interpreted as regex syntax instead of a literal character.

The most practical case is  `.` , which GitHub allows in org/repo names and is a regex wildcard meaning "any single character." For example, an attacker-controlled repository named:

`github/artifact.attestations-workflows`

matches a verifier configured for the trusted signer:

`github/artifact-attestations-workflows`

because the unescaped  `.`  in the constructed pattern matches the  `-`  in the attacker's name (and any other single character at that position). This affected the `--signer-repo` and `--signer-workflow` flags but did not affect the `--repo` and `--owner` flags which include an exact string comparison.

In `v2.97.0`, the GitHub CLI escapes the user-supplied signer values before they are incorporated into the SAN matcher, so they are matched as literal strings.

### Impact

The practical impact is limited, exploitation requires the attacker to create a plausible lookalike repository name and produce valid Sigstore attestations from it. This could undermine supply chain verification for CI/CD pipelines or policy gates that use these flags to pin trust to a specific signing workflow. 

### Remediation and Mitigation

1. Upgrade `gh` to `v2.97.0` or later, which escapes signer values before matching.
2. As a workaround, use `--repo` or `--owner` flags instead of `--signer-repo` or `--signer-workflow` where applicable.
3. Manually inspect the signing certificate SAN in attestation output to confirm the signing workflow origin.

### Summary

A path traversal vulnerability has been identified in the GitHub CLI where some HTTP request URLs, REST API calls in particular, were built without properly escaping their variable path components. A value containing URL path metacharacters can alter the request path and cause `gh` to address a different resource than intended.

### Details

Not all request URLs in the codebase were built with proper escaping of their variable path components. When a component is interpolated into the path without percent encoding, and that component contains URL path metacharacters, it breaks out of its intended segment and changes the effective request path.

In `2.97.0`, request URLs are constructed in a safe manner, so a variable component can no longer escape its intended segment.

### Impact

An attacker who can control a value that flows into a request path can cause `gh` to send the request to a different API endpoint than intended. This can lead the CLI to read or act on a resource other than the one the user meant to target.

### Remediation and Mitigation

1. Upgrade `gh` to `2.97.0`.
2. Be cautious when running `gh` against untrusted repositories or inputs whose names you do not control.

cves.summary:
### Summary

A security vulnerability has been identified in GitHub CLI where `gh auth status` could potentially print a portion of the authentication token in plaintext, depending on the lexical structure of the token.

Affected users:
- Authenticated users who ran `gh auth status` (without the `--show-token` flag) with a token type whose format contains an underscore after the prefix. This includes fine-grained personal access tokens (`github_pat_*`) and GitHub App installation/user access tokens (`ghs_*`, `ghu_*`, e.g., `ghs_<APPID>_<JWT>`), including the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Classic tokens such as `gho_*` and `ghp_*` have an underscore-free body and are not affected.

### Details

The vulnerability stems from the way GitHub CLI masks the authentication token when reporting authentication state:

1. A user runs `gh auth status` without `--show-token`, expecting the token to be fully masked.
2. The masking logic redacts only the characters that follow the last underscore in the token, instead of redacting everything after the token prefix.
3. The partially masked token is written to the command output, where it can be captured or shared.

Because `gh auth status` is a diagnostic command commonly run interactively and inside automated environments, the leaked token characters can end up in CI/CD job logs, terminal scrollback, screen recordings, screenshots, or pasted output shared in bug reports and support requests.

In `v2.97.0`, GitHub CLI fully masks the token in `gh auth status` output, preserving only the known token prefix and redacting the remainder unless `--show-token` is explicitly provided.

### Impact

Running `gh auth status` in a context where the output is captured, logged, or shared could leak a portion of an affected token. The affected token types are fine-grained personal access tokens (`github_pat_*`) and GitHub App installation/user access tokens (`ghs_*`, `ghu_*`, e.g., `ghs_<APPID>_<JWT>`), including the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Installation and Actions tokens are short-lived, which narrows the window in which a recovered token could be reused. See [GitHub credential types](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-programmatic-access-to-your-organization/github-credential-types#credential-types-overview).

### Remediation and Mitigation

1. Upgrade `gh` to `v2.97.0`.
2. Rotate any affected token whose masked `gh auth status` output may have been captured or shared:
   - **Fine-grained personal access tokens (`github_pat_*`):** regenerate the token from your account settings. See [Managing your personal access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens).
   - **GitHub App installation/user access tokens (`ghs_*`, `ghu_*`, e.g., `ghs_<APPID>_<JWT>`):** these are short-lived and rotate automatically (See [GitHub credential types](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-programmatic-access-to-your-organization/github-credential-types#credential-types-overview)). If you believe a token was captured while still valid, you can revoke it immediately using the [Revoke an installation access token](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/apps/installations#revoke-an-installation-access-token) REST endpoint (`DELETE /installation/token`). To cut off a third-party app's access more broadly, suspend or uninstall the app from the web UI. See [Reviewing and modifying installed GitHub Apps](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/using-github-apps/reviewing-and-modifying-installed-github-apps).
   - **Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN`:** this token is automatically invalidated when the job finishes, so no manual revocation is normally required. See [GitHub credential types](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/managing-programmatic-access-to-your-organization/github-credential-types#credential-types-overview).
3. Until you can upgrade, avoid running `gh auth status` in contexts where the output is captured or shared, and manually redact the token line before sharing any output.
